theme: O God, do not keep silence
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 83. It is a prayer against a coalition of enemy nations that plot to wipe Israel off the map. Notice what the psalmist finally asks God to do to the enemies, and why.
settingTheScene: Psalm 83 is a song of Asaph. It lists ten nations that have conspired against Israel: Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre, and Assyria. The occasion may be one of the great coalitions in Judah’s history, such as the one in 2 Chronicles 20. It follows the oracles against the nations: those who plot against God’s people will answer to God.
observation: “O God, do not keep silence; do not hold your peace or be still, O God!” (v. 1).
“For behold, your enemies make an uproar; those who hate you have raised their heads” (v. 2).
“They lay crafty plans against your people; they consult together against your treasured ones” (v. 3).
“They say, Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more!” (v. 4).
“For they conspire with one accord; against you they make a covenant” (v. 5).
“Do to them as you did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon” (v. 9).
“Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD” (v. 16).
“That they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth” (v. 18).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with an urgent plea that God would not be silent. The psalmist feels that God is quiet while the enemies are loud. This is the common experience of the people of God: the wicked are noisy and active, and God seems to be still. The prayer asks God to speak and act.

The enemies’ plan is genocide. “Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more!” It is a conspiracy to erase God’s people. Notice the key line in verse 5: “Against you they make a covenant.” The psalmist sees that the attack on Israel is an attack on God. The people are God’s treasured ones, and to threaten them is to threaten him. This is the same logic as Saul on the road to Damascus, who was asked, “Why are you persecuting me?”

The psalmist then recalls past victories: Midian, Sisera, Jabin, Oreb and Zeeb. These were not won by Israel’s strength but by God’s intervention. The memory of past deliverance is the ground of present prayer.

The prayer for judgment uses imagery of fire, wind, and storms: let them be like tumbleweed, like chaff before the wind, like a forest in flames. But look at the purpose. “Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD.” The aim is not only destruction but conversion. The psalmist wants the enemies to be humbled so that they will seek God. And the final goal is universal: “that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth.”

This is the true motive of all faithful prayer for justice: the glory of God and the knowing of his name across the earth.
connection: In Acts 9:4, Jesus asked Saul, “Why are you persecuting me?” Saul, once an enemy, became an apostle, just as the psalm hopes enemies may seek the LORD’s name. Matthew 5:44 commands us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us. Philippians 2:10-11 says that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Revelation 11:15 says the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord.
application:
Pray for those who oppose the church, that they would seek the name of the LORD.

Remember a past deliverance and give thanks. Let it support a present prayer.

Pray for the persecuted church by name, if you know a country or region.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what troubles his people today.
Ask him to act, and to bring his enemies to seek his name.
Remember what he has done in the past.
